LESSONS.title: Keys and values
LESSONS.goal: Make a dictionary and get a value out by its key
summary: {key: value} pairs a lookup word with a value
Get a value with menu[key]; a missing key is a KeyError
It prints like {'latte': 4000}

cards.say: A dictionary is a box that stores pairs: a key (the word you look up) and a value. Write key: value pairs inside curly braces, separated by commas, and get a value with menu[key]. Lists look things up by number; dictionaries look them up by name.

Print a whole dictionary and it usually shows up with single quotes, like {'latte': 4000}. Ask for a key that isn't there and you get a KeyError clue. The clue even names the key you were looking for.

items.q: What's the output?
items.code:
menu = {"latte": 4000, "mocha": 4500}
print(menu["latte"])
items.explain: menu["latte"] gets the value paired with latte. That value is 4000, so 4000 shows up.

items.q: Which clue (error) do you get when you run this code?
items.code:
menu = {"latte": 4000}
print(menu["mocha"])
items.explain: Asking a dictionary for a key it doesn't have gives a KeyError. IndexError is for list numbers that go out of range.

items.q: Fill in the blank so the mocha price, 4500, is printed.
items.code:
menu = {"latte": 4000, "mocha": 4500}
print(menu[___])
items.explain: The key is a string, so it needs quotes. Without quotes Python reads it as a variable name (NameError), and 4500 isn't a key (KeyError).

items.q: What's the output?
items.code:
price = {"latte": 4000}
print(price)
items.explain: Printing a whole dictionary keeps the curly braces and quotes. Python usually shows strings with single quotes.

items.q: Put the lines in order so the latte price, 4000, is printed.
items.explain: Make the dictionary first, then take the value out into p, then print it. Taking it out before the dictionary exists is a NameError.

items.task: Make a dictionary called menu (americano 3000, latte 4000, mocha 4500). Read a menu name with input() (leave the parentheses empty) and print its price with menu[name]. Example: entering latte prints 4000
hints: Print the one price that matches the name you typed. In the example, why does latte give 4000?
Make a dictionary with {key: value} and read it with menu[key]. You can put a variable in the key spot.
Pair the three drinks with their prices in menu, then use the name you read as the key and print what comes out.

menu = {"americano": ___,
        "latte": 4000, "mocha": 4500}
name = input()
print(menu[___])
items.explain: Grabbing a value straight by its key is what dictionaries are great at. No long chain of ifs, just one line.

items.q: menu has no key "cookie". What happens with menu["cookie"]?
items.explain: Reading with [ ] stops with a KeyError when the key is missing. The error-free way is get, which is coming up soon.

LESSONS.title: Add and change
LESSONS.goal: Add and change values, and check keys with in
summary: d[key] = value: adds if missing, replaces if there
Keys never repeat; each key appears only once
key in d checks keys only; an empty box is {}
If the value is a list, use d[k].append(value)

cards.say: Writing d[key] = value adds the pair if the key is new, and changes the value if the key is already there. A key only exists once, so putting in the same key again wipes out the old value.
key in dictionary tells you True or False: is that key there? It only looks at keys, not values. Make an empty dictionary with {}. not in asks if it's missing.
cards.code:
stock = {}
stock["apple"] = 3
print("apple" in stock)
print(3 in stock)

cards.say: A dictionary's values can be lists too. When a key is new, first give it an empty list, then pile things up with scores[key].append(value).

items.q: What's the output?
items.explain: Putting a value under a new key adds a new pair at the end. The apple pair that was already there stays.

items.q: What's the output?
items.explain: The right side is worked out first: 3 + 2 = 5. Then that goes back under the same key, so it becomes 5.

items.q: What's the output?
items.code:
stock = {"apple": 3}
print(3 in stock)
items.explain: in looks for keys, not values. 3 is a value, not a key, so it's False. No error happens.

items.q: Fill in the blank so it prints “no”.
items.explain: pear isn't a key, so "pear" in stock is False and we go to else. not in flips it and prints “yes”.

items.q: Put the lines in order so {'plum': 5} is printed.
items.explain: Make an empty box, put plum in as 4, then add 1 and put it back. Reading it before it's added is a KeyError.

items.q: What's the output?
items.code:
stock = {}
stock["apple"] = 1
stock["apple"] = 2
print(stock)
items.explain: A key exists only once, so putting in the same key again replaces the value. Only the last one, 2, is left.

items.q: What's the output?
items.explain: Minji shows up twice, so the empty list is made only the first time and 1 is added twice. Jun shows up once, so [1].

items.task: stock has apple 3 and pear 5. Read a fruit name with input() (leave the parentheses empty), set it with stock[name] = 10, then print stock. Example: entering grape prints {'apple': 3, 'pear': 5, 'grape': 10}
hints: Make the stock of the fruit you typed 10, then print all of stock. What if the fruit is already there?
d[key] = value adds if missing and replaces if there. The same single line handles both.
Use the item you read as the key and 10 as the value. Then print stock as a whole.

stock = {"apple": 3, "pear": 5}
item = input()
stock[___] = ___
print(stock)
items.explain: A new fruit gets added and an existing one changes to 10. One line covers both cases, no if needed. Neat!

items.q: What does stock["pear"] = 7 do?
options: Adds pear if missing, changes its value if there
Causes a KeyError if pear is already there
Does nothing if pear is missing
items.explain: Assigning creates the key if it's missing and overwrites it if it's there. KeyError only happens when you read a missing key.

LESSONS.title: get and looping
LESSONS.goal: Read safely with get and loop over a dictionary
summary: get(key, default): default if missing, no error
for k in d: gives you the keys
items gives keys and values; values gives values only

cards.say: get(key, default) gives the value if the key is there, and the default instead of a KeyError if it isn't. Leave out the default and you get None when the key is missing.
cards.code:
menu = {"latte": 4000}
print(menu.get("latte", "sold out"))
print(menu.get("mocha", "sold out"))
print(menu.get("mocha"))

cards.say: Looping over a dictionary with for gives you the keys, not the values. To get keys and values together, write for k, v in d.items():. values() gathers just the values, and sum works on it too.

items.q: What's the output?
items.code:
menu = {"latte": 4000}
print(menu.get("mocha", "sold out"))
items.explain: mocha isn't a key, so you get the default, "sold out". Reading with [ ] would have been a KeyError.

items.q: What's the output?
items.code:
menu = {"latte": 4000}
print(menu.get("mocha"))
items.explain: Without a default, a missing key gives None. There's no error; None just means "no value".

items.q: What's the output?
items.explain: Looping over a dictionary with for gives only the keys. If you want the values too, use items().

items.q: Fill in the blank so each key is printed with its value.
items.explain: items() gives a key and a value as a pair. keys() gives one key at a time and values() one value at a time, so they can't be split into k, v.

items.q: Put the lines in order so the total price, 8500, is printed.
items.explain: Make the dictionary, gather just the values with values() and add them up, then print. A different order is a NameError.

items.task: Put latte 4000 and mocha 4500 in menu. Read a menu name with input() (leave the parentheses empty) and print its price with get, or “sold out” if it's not on the menu. Example: entering cookie prints “sold out”
hints: Print the price for drinks on the menu and “sold out” for anything else. In the example, why is cookie sold out?
get(key, default) gives the default instead of an error when the key is missing. The default can be a string.
Call get with name as the key and sold out in the default spot, then print the result.
items.explain: One get line handled both cases, with no if and in. Even a drink that isn't on the menu gives sold out instead of a KeyError.

items.q: With menu = {"latte": 4000}, what is menu.get("mocha", 0) + 1?
items.explain: mocha is missing, so get gives the default 0, and adding 1 makes 1. This little sum is next lesson's counting pattern.

LESSONS.title: The counting pattern
LESSONS.goal: Count words and letters with a dictionary
summary: Get an empty box ready first: counts = {}
counts[w] = counts.get(w, 0) + 1
A new key starts from get's default, 0

cards.say: Here's the counting pattern. Make an empty dictionary, and on each pass do counts[w] = counts.get(w, 0) + 1. A new word gets 0 from get and becomes 1; a word you've seen goes up by 1 each time.
Letters work the same way. Looping over a string with for gives one letter at a time. Show the result line by line with for k, v in counts.items():.

items.q: What's the output?
items.explain: tea appears twice, so 2, and coffee once, so 1. Keys go in the order they first appear.

items.q: Which clue (error) do you get when you run this code?
items.explain: The first bun isn't in counts yet, so reading counts[w] is a KeyError. Read it with get(w, 0) instead.

items.q: Fill in the blank so bun is counted 2 times.
items.explain: The first time, 0 + 1 should start it at 1. With 1 it starts at 2 and ends at 3, and None can't be added, so it's a TypeError.

items.q: Put the lines in order so {'tea': 2, 'bun': 1} is printed.
items.explain: Make the empty box first, count inside the loop, and print after the loop ends. Making the box too late is a NameError.

items.q: What's the output?
items.explain: Looping over the string gives a, a, b in turn. a twice and b once makes {'a': 2, 'b': 1}.

items.task: Read votes on one line, separated by spaces, with input() (leave the parentheses empty), split() them, and count each candidate's votes in the empty dictionary counts using get. Print “candidate votes” one per line, in the order they first appear. Example: A B A prints “A 2” and “B 1” on two lines
hints: Count how many votes each candidate got, then print one line each in the order they first appeared. In A B A, why does A get 2?
It's the counting pattern. On each pass, add up with counts[candidate] = counts.get(candidate, 0) + 1.
After the loop, use a second for that goes over keys and values together to print each line. Put the name and the count in print together.
items.explain: Keeping the counting loop and the showing loop apart is clean. It works with just one vote and with votes in a mixed-up order.

items.q: The first time a word shows up, what does counts.get(w, 0) give?
items.explain: The key isn't there yet, so you get the default 0. Add 1, save it, and the first count is 1.

LESSONS.title: Chapter 8 checkpoint
LESSONS.goal: Use every dictionary skill to tally orders
summary: d[key] is a KeyError if missing; get gives a default
d[key] = value adds or replaces
Count with d[w] = d.get(w, 0) + 1

cards.say: Chapter 8 checkpoint! Getting by key, adding and changing, reading safely with get, and the counting pattern all come back. Take it slow and you'll do great.

items.q: Which clue (error) do you get when you run this code?
items.code:
menu = {"latte": 4000}
print(menu["cookie"])
items.explain: Reading a missing key with [ ] is a KeyError. None is what you get with get.

items.q: What's the output?
items.code:
cart = {"bread": 2}
cart["milk"] = 1
cart["bread"] = 5
print(cart)
items.explain: milk gets added, and bread is the same key, so it's replaced with 5. Keys never repeat.

items.q: Fill in the blank so it prints “gone”.
items.code:
menu = {"latte": 4000}
print(menu.get("cookie", ___))
items.explain: The default is a string, so it needs quotes. Without quotes, Python reads gone as a variable name, so it's a NameError. And menu would print the whole dictionary.

items.q: What's the output?
items.explain: Looping over a dictionary with for gives the keys. To get the values too, use items().

items.q: Put the lines in order so {'milk': 2, 'bread': 1} is printed.
items.explain: Make the empty box, count in the loop, print after the loop. The counting line must be indented inside the for.

items.q: Fill in the blank so each key and value is printed as a pair.
items.explain: To get keys and values together, use items(). keys() gives only one key at a time, so it can't be split into k, v.

items.q: What's the output?
items.code:
cart = {"bread": 2}
print("milk" in cart)
items.explain: in only tells you whether the key is there. milk isn't a key, so it's False, and no error happens.

items.task: menu is latte 4000, mocha 4500. Read orders separated by spaces with input() (leave the parentheses empty), keep only the ones on the menu using if and in, and count them in counts with get. Print “item quantity” one per line in first-seen order, then “Total amount” last. Example: latte mocha latte → “latte 2” “mocha 1” “Total 12500”
hints: Count only the orders that are on the menu, then print the quantity lines and a total line. In the example, where does 12500 come from?
For each order, if it's not on the menu (not in), skip it with continue. If it is, count it with get and add its price to total.
After the counting loop, print each line with counts.items(), then print the total line last using total.
items.explain: Filtering with in, counting with get, and reading prices by key all clicked together. Even when none of the orders are on the menu, it ends cleanly with Total 0.

items.q: In counts[w] = counts.get(w, 0) + 1, what's the main reason to use get?
options: To avoid a KeyError on a new word
To delete a word that's already there
items.explain: A new key isn't there yet, so reading it with [ ] is a KeyError. get's default 0 fills that gap.

ADVANCED.title: Group and count
ADVANCED.goal: Group words by a feature, then count or add them up
summary: Use w[0] or len(w) as the key instead of w to change the rule
Label with if, then use that label as the key
Add a value instead of 1 to get a total, not a count

cards.say: This is where we go one step further. You don't need it to unlock the next chapter. In 8-4 we counted whole words, right? Switch the key to w[0] (the first letter) and you count by first letter.
Add a value instead of 1 and you get a total. The rule can come from an if too: 5000 won or more is “pricey”, otherwise “normal”, and that label becomes the key for adding up the prices.

items.q: What's the output?
items.explain: The key is the first letter, so bread and bun pile up in the same “b” slot and make 2. Keys go in the order they first appear.

items.q: What's the output?
items.explain: The letter count is the key. 3 letters: tea and pie, two. 4 letters: milk, cake and soda, three. Number keys still print in first-seen order (3 first).

items.q: Fill in the blank so the words are counted by first letter.
items.explain: w[0] is the first letter, so all three land under “b”. Using w counts each word separately, and w[1] groups by the second letter instead.

items.q: Put the lines in order so {4: 3} is printed.
items.explain: Make the box first, find the letter count and count it inside the loop, then print after the loop. Using n before it's set is a NameError.

items.q: What's the output?
items.explain: 2000 goes into normal, and 6000 and 7000 add up in pricey: 6000 + 7000 = 13000. If you added 1 instead, you'd get counts.

items.task: Read words separated by spaces with input() (leave the parentheses empty) and count them by letter count (len) with get. Gather them in counts, then print “length n: k” one per line in first-seen order. Example: tea pie milk → “length 3: 2” “length 4: 1”
hints: Count words with the same number of letters together, not the same word, then print from the first length you saw. In tea pie milk, why does length 3 have 2?
Take the counting pattern from 8-4 and change only the key. Use len(w) instead of the word w, and you count by length.
In the first loop, find the length and count it with get. After the loop, use a second for over keys and values together and print an f-string.
items.explain: You only swapped the key for len(w) in the counting pattern, and the rule changed. It works with a single word and when every word has the same length.

items.q: In sums.get(k, 0) + p, if you add p instead of 1, what piles up?
options: The total amount for each group
The biggest value for each group
items.explain: Adding 1 counts how many times something appeared; adding p sums up all the p values. Same skeleton, only the added value changes.

ADVANCED.title: Lists inside a dictionary
ADVANCED.goal: Collect values into a list for each group and use them
summary: For a new key, first set d[k] = [] (an empty list)
Pile values up per group with d[k].append(value)
Use [0], len or sum directly on the list you get out

cards.say: One more step! In 8-2 you got a taste of dictionaries whose values are lists. Instead of counting, pile up the words themselves and you get groups by first letter. Only make an empty list when the key is new.
The value you get out is a list, so you can put an index right after it or use len and sum. scores[name][1] is that person's second score.

items.q: What's the output?
items.code:
d = {"Minji": [90, 80], "Jun": [70]}
print(d["Minji"][1])
items.explain: d["Minji"] is the list [90, 80], and adding [1] gives the second item, 80. Indexes start at 0.

items.q: What's the output?
items.explain: scores["Jun"] is a list, so append adds 100 at the end. What's printed is just that one list, not the dictionary.

items.q: Fill in the blank so x gets two 1s piled up.
items.explain: To use append, the value has to be a list. 0 and {} don't have append, so you'd get an AttributeError.

items.q: Put the lines in order so 1 is printed.
items.explain: Empty dictionary, empty list, add a score, count them. Appending before the list exists is a KeyError.

items.q: What's the output?
items.code:
scores = {"Minji": [90, 80]}
print(sum(scores["Minji"]))
items.explain: scores["Minji"] gives a list, so sum can add it up: 90 + 80 = 170.

items.task: Read names on the first line and scores on the second (same order) with input() (leave the parentheses empty), and append each score to that name's list in groups. Turn scores into numbers with int(). Print “name [scores]” in first-seen order. Example: “Minji Jun Minji” “90 70 80” → “Minji [90, 80]” “Jun [70]”
hints: Gather the scores of the same name into one list. If Minji shows up twice, how many scores go in Minji's list?
A name and a score with the same index belong together (range(len(a)) from 7-2). If the key is new, make an empty list first, then append.
Loop with an index i, use names[i] as the key and append int(scores[i]). After the loop, go over keys and values together and print.
items.explain: Making an empty list only for new names and then piling up scores is a clean flow. It works with one person and with names in a mixed-up order.

items.q: Before d[k].append(x), why set d[k] = [] first when the key is new?
options: Reading a missing key with d[k] is a KeyError
To erase the values already there
items.explain: d[k].append(x) reads d[k] first, and a missing key is a KeyError. Putting in an empty list first makes that read work.

ADVANCED.title: Report card summary
ADVANCED.goal: Find each person's average and the top scorer
summary: Average: round(sum(v) / len(v), 1)
For the highest value, compare with > and swap it in
Grouping, counting and comparing in one program

cards.say: Last Deep Dive lesson! Let's find averages from each person's score list. Divide the sum by the count, then use round to keep just one decimal place.
Find the top scorer with an if inside the loop. If an average beats the best so far, swap it in. Because it's >, on a tie the person who came first stays.

items.q: What's the output?
items.code:
v = [70, 85]
print(round(sum(v) / len(v), 1))
items.explain: The sum 155 divided by the count 2 is 77.5. round(…, 1) keeps one decimal place, and it already has just one, so it stays.

items.q: What's the output?
items.explain: The first score, 55, is a fail, so the fail key goes in first. 70 and 90 pass, 40 fails, so two each.

items.q: Fill in the blank so the highest average, 88.0, is printed.
items.explain: Only swap in when it's bigger than the best so far. With < or == it never swaps, so -1 is printed. We start at -1 so even a 0 can win.

items.q: Put the lines in order so 80.0 is printed.
items.explain: Make the score list, find the average, then round and print. Using avg before it's found is a NameError.

items.q: What's the output?
items.explain: A becomes the best first with 70.0. B is only equal, not bigger, so it doesn't get swapped in. On a tie, whoever came first stays.

items.task: Read names on the first line and scores on the second (same order) with input() (leave the parentheses empty) and append them by name into groups. Print “name average” in first-seen order (sum, len, round, one decimal place), then “Top name” at the end using if. On a tie, the first one wins. Example: Minji Jun Minji / 90 70 80 → Minji 85.0, Jun 70.0, Top Minji
hints: Gather scores by name and find each average, then print the person with the highest average last. In the example, why is Minji's average 85.0?
Build groups with the grouping from A2. In the loop, find and print each average while comparing it with the best so far.
Start the best average at -1 and the best name as an empty string. If an average beats the best, swap both. On a tie, leave them.

(after grouping)
best_name = ""
best_avg = -1
for k, v in groups.items():
    avg = round(sum(v) / len(v), 1)
    print(k, avg)
    if avg ___ best_avg:
        best_avg = avg
        best_name = ___
print("Top", best_name)
items.solution:
names = input().split()
scores = input().split()
groups = {}
for i in range(len(names)):
    n = names[i]
    if n not in groups:
        groups[n] = []
    groups[n].append(int(scores[i]))
best_name = ""
best_avg = -1
for k, v in groups.items():
    avg = round(sum(v) / len(v), 1)
    print(k, avg)
    if avg > best_avg:
        best_avg = avg
        best_name = k
print("Top", best_name)
items.explain: Grouping, averaging and finding the best, all in one flow. It works with a score of 0, with ties, and with long decimals.

items.q: If the if that finds the best average uses > instead of >=, who stays on a tie?
items.explain: > only swaps when it's truly bigger. On a tie nothing is swapped, so the one who came first stays.

TEMPLATES.q: A fruit price list. What's the output?
TEMPLATES.explain: A dictionary gets values by key, not by number. Using a key that isn't there gives a KeyError.

TEMPLATES.q: Fill in the blank so you get 0 instead of an error when there's no “{X}” key.
TEMPLATES.explain: get(key, default) gives back the default when the key is missing. With 0 as the default you get 0; with None or text, you get that instead.

TEMPLATES.q: You bought {N} more apples. What's the output?
TEMPLATES.explain: Just calculating leaves the dictionary as it was. You have to put the result back into stock["apple"] to change it, and plain = with only the new number loses the old value.

TEMPLATES.q: Count how many times each word appears. What's the output?
TEMPLATES.explain: get(w, 0) + 1 starts a new word at 0 and adds 1. counts[w] = 1 overwrites with 1 every time, and += on a missing key is a KeyError.

TEMPLATES.q: Put two names in the {K} team. What's the output?
wrong:
groups = {}
groups["{K}"] = []
groups["{K}"].append("{A}")
groups["{K}"] = []
groups["{K}"].append("{B}")
print(groups["{K}"])
TEMPLATES.explain: You need an empty list first before you can use append. Skip it and you get a KeyError; put [] in again and the first name disappears.
